title: How Exposed Are You? A Data Broker Reality Check
excerpt: Most people don't know their data is already on sale. Here's where it is, what it costs, and what you can do about it.
content:
The Hidden Market for Your Information

Every day, your personal data is bought, sold, and traded in marketplaces you'll never see. Data brokers collect information from public records, online transactions, social media, and thousands of other sources—then repackage and sell it to advertisers, scammers, and worse.

The scale is staggering: the data brokerage industry processes billions of records annually. Your name, address, phone number, email, age, income level, web browsing habits, purchase history, and even your political leanings are commodities with a price tag.

Where Does Your Data Go?

Your exposure isn't random. It follows predictable paths:

  • Public Records: Court filings, property deeds, voter registration, business licenses—all searchable and harvestable by brokers.
  • Online Services: Every account you create (social media, email, shopping) is a data point. Many services sell anonymized (or not-so-anonymized) user profiles to third parties.
  • Data Aggregators: Companies like Acxiom, Experian, and Epsilon buy raw data from dozens of sources, then enhance it with inferences and predictions.
  • Advertising Networks: Google, Facebook, and programmatic ad platforms track your browsing to build detailed profiles—then sell access to that targeting to advertisers.
  • Forgotten Accounts: Old social profiles, websites you signed up for years ago, services you no longer use—many still hold your data and sell or share it forward.

Why This Matters (Beyond Privacy)

Exposed data isn't just a privacy issue. It's a safety and financial one:

  • Identity Theft: Criminals buy datasets to fuel phishing, account takeovers, and fraud.
  • Targeted Harassment: Your address, phone number, and employer become tools for stalking and intimidation.
  • Discrimination: Brokers sell inferred data (income level, creditworthiness, health) that can affect lending, employment, and insurance decisions.
  • Manipulation: Your psychological profile is sold to political campaigns and bad actors for microtargeted manipulation.

What You Can Actually Do

The good news: your data exposure isn't permanent. Most data brokers honor removal requests—they're just not required to make it easy.

  • Step 1: Know Your Exposure – Start with a free privacy scan. See which brokers have your data and what they know.
  • Step 2: Remove Systematically – File removal requests with each broker. Some do it manually (slow), some offer bulk removal (faster).
  • Step 3: Monitor and Maintain – New data enters broker databases constantly. Periodic checks catch re-listings.

The Path Forward

Privacy isn't a product—it's a process. Understanding where your data is today is the first step toward controlling it tomorrow.

Start with a scan. See what's out there. Then take it back, piece by piece.

title: GDPR vs CCPA: What Privacy Rights Do You Actually Have?
excerpt: Two major privacy laws. One applies to Europe, one to California. But what if you're neither? Here's what you need to know.
content:
The Global Privacy Patchwork

Privacy law is fractured. There's no single "global standard"—instead, we have competing regional frameworks that apply based on where you live or where companies operate.

The two heavyweights are GDPR (Europe) and CCPA (California). Together, they've influenced privacy regulation worldwide and set a baseline for what companies can (and can't) do with your data.

But the details matter. And they're very different.

GDPR: The European Hammer

The General Data Protection Regulation applies to anyone in the EU, plus any company anywhere that collects data from EU residents. It's broad, strict, and penalties are severe (up to €20 million or 4% of global revenue).

Your Rights Under GDPR

  • Right to Access: You can request all data a company holds on you. They must respond within 30 days.
  • Right to Erasure ("Right to Be Forgotten"): You can demand deletion of your data in most cases.
  • Right to Rectification: Inaccurate data must be corrected.
  • Right to Restrict Processing: You can limit how companies use your data.
  • Right to Portability: Your data in machine-readable format so you can move to another service.
  • Right to Object: Say no to processing for marketing, profiling, or automated decisions.

CCPA: The California Shortcut

The California Consumer Privacy Act is newer and narrower than GDPR. It only applies in California, and only to for-profit companies doing business there with annual revenues over $25 million—or collecting data from 100,000+ people.

But it's stricter in one way: it gives you a right to opt-out of the sale or sharing of your data, not just its collection.

Your Rights Under CCPA

  • Right to Know: What data is collected, used, and shared.
  • Right to Delete: Request deletion (with some exceptions).
  • Right to Opt-Out: Stop the sale or sharing of your personal information.
  • Right to Correct: Fix inaccurate data.
  • Right to Non-Discrimination: Companies can't penalize you for exercising your privacy rights.

What If You're Neither in Europe Nor California?

Good question. Most of the world lacks comprehensive privacy law. But momentum is building:

  • PDPO (Hong Kong): Moderate protection, covers residents and visitors.
  • PDPA (Thailand, Singapore, others): Emerging frameworks, generally weaker than GDPR.
  • LGPD (Brazil): Similar to GDPR in scope, heavy penalties for violations.

If you're in an unprotected jurisdiction, you still have leverage: most global companies apply GDPR-like standards globally because compliance is cheaper than maintaining separate systems.

How to Exercise Your Rights

On paper, it's simple. In practice, it's tedious.

  • Start with a Subject Access Request (SAR): Contact the company directly and ask for all data they hold on you. Frame it under the law that applies to you (GDPR if you're in EU; CCPA if in California; or use GDPR regardless—many companies honor it globally).
  • Document Everything: Save copies of your request and their response. If they ignore you, that's evidence.
  • Escalate If Needed: If the company ignores your request, file a complaint with your data protection authority (like the ICO in the UK or CPRA in California).

The Takeaway

Privacy law is imperfect and fragmented. But it exists. Your rights exist. The only reason companies don't respect them is because most people don't ask.

Ask. Document. Escalate if needed. It works.
